prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect, and the Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant topological insulators

statement.case_for: I keep B045 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and I have not changed my configuration since round 1. The chair asked whether the citation can stand without the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, the 3D strand and the quantum anomalous Hall strand. I think it can if it is tied to what these three people did: Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant and predicted the quantum spin Hall state with its helical edge channels, and Molenkamp's group showed quantised edge conduction in HgTe quantum wells, with nonlocal measurements later establishing the edge-channel picture. That is a closed theory-to-experiment arc with a distinct physical mechanism, time-reversal symmetry rather than a broken-symmetry quantum Hall state, and it has been reproduced and extended for fifteen years. The conceptual consequence, that band topology classifies insulators and protects boundary states, is the broadest of any shortlisted entry and is already part of how condensed matter is taught and how materials are searched. On the 2016 question, I keep my view that the earlier prize concerned topological phase transitions and quantised Hall conductance in systems with broken time-reversal symmetry, so the physics honoured here is different even if the word topology recurs.
statement.case_against: The credit tree remains incomplete, and I do not think wording fully repairs it. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal directed Molenkamp's experiment, Zhang is deceased, and three names cannot represent Fu, Hasan, Xue and others. A citation can make the claim narrower, but it cannot make the omission disappear, and Olsson is right to treat this as a real fairness cost. The 2016 prize also leaves a legitimate worry that the committee will read a second topology award as a close follow-up. Against B022, I accept that a clean two-name attribution and a very mature reproduction record are strengths B045 does not match. If the committee concludes that attribution clarity should decide, B022 is a defensible outcome and I would vote for it over any three-name topology configuration that adds Xue or Hasan.

responses.point: Pearce asked whether the four-way credit problem in topological insulators can be solved with three names without a visible injustice, and noted that B004 and B045 split the same story into incompatible credit sets.
responses.response: I cannot claim a solution without injustice. What I can claim is that a quantum spin Hall prize is internally coherent while B004 is not, because B004 combines the spin Hall effect with Xue's quantum anomalous Hall effect, which needs magnetic doping and is a separate achievement. That is why I dropped Xue and why I now treat B004 only as a version to avoid. The residual injustice is Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and I would say so in the public wording of the citation by limiting it to the prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect in graphene and its first observation. I agree with the chair's fragmentation point, and it is a reason to settle on one configuration, B045, and not to count B004 support as support for the same prize.

responses.point: Kroll holds B022 first for its clean two-person credit and independent confirmation, and noted that my earlier Kane-Molenkamp pairing for B004 was a cleaner configuration than the three-name version.
responses.response: I accept that B022 is cleaner and I do not dispute its maturity. Where we differ is the criterion. A prize should recognise the discovery or invention that most changed physics, and for me that is the concept of topological band structure, which reaches beyond one measurement regime. I also take Kroll's point about my earlier pairing, but I have decided that Kane-Molenkamp without Mele is not defensible, since Mele co-authored the Z2 theory in the same two papers. So the cleaner pairing is not a fallback I would pursue. Kroll's disclosed Hall-laboratory stay is worth the committee noting for B022, but I treat it as a disclosed bias and not a reason to discount his scientific argument.

responses.point: Olsson argues that the overlap of lattice clocks with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is narrow, since ensemble interrogation at a magic wavelength is new, and treats the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission as a fairness cost against B045.
responses.response: I agree with Olsson on the clock overlap. The magic-wavelength ensemble idea is a distinct step, and I would not oppose B022 on that ground. That is why I list it as my first alternative. On the cost of omitting Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, I accept the fairness point, but I see it as a limit of the three-person rule that applies to every shortlisted topology configuration. The B022 credit tail (Lemonde, Takamoto, the Yb and Hg groups) is a similar limit. I do not regard either tail as decisive, so the choice between B045 and B022 depends on how the committee weighs conceptual breadth against attribution clarity, not on which ballot has the smaller omission.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B030 as a sharp prediction followed by an unexpected experiment, and argued that the unfinished theory of the correlated phases should not disqualify it. Danielsson also noted my own B039 proximity to the 2025 circuit prize.
responses.response: I agree that an unfinished theory of the phases is not disqualifying in itself, and the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is a strong sequence. My hesitation is timing: about eight years in, with the pairing mechanism and the sensitivity to twist-angle disorder still debated, I would rather wait than award before the interpretation settles. I would not block B030 in a later year and I keep it as an alternative. On B039, I agree that two quantum-circuit prizes in consecutive years would look repetitive, and I would recuse myself in any case, so it does not enter my configuration.

responses.point: Mehlig supports the same Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio, and argued that the quantum anomalous Hall effect is a realisation of a different effect that should not be mixed into the citation.
responses.response: I agree and have taken the Xue point fully on board. Mehlig's remark about the robustness of the topological invariant is also the central reason for my position, because it makes the result an organising principle and not a model-dependent claim. I would add that applications remain mostly prospective, which I treat as secondary since the prize recognises the discovery and not its use.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the 2016 topological-phases prize concerned different physics, since this is the main risk to B045 and my view rests on my own reading of the distinction.

Whether a citation limited to the prediction and first observation of the quantum spin Hall effect is enough to answer the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, or whether the omission will be judged an injustice whatever the wording.
How much weight breadth of conceptual influence should carry against clear attribution when the two point to different ballots.
I rely on my own background knowledge of the priority history and have not verified it independently.
statement.conflict_note: I work in superconducting circuits, direct WACQT at Chalmers, which hosted several researchers linked to the 2025 prize, and have a documented collaborative link to Chalmers colleagues such as Per Delsing. I would recuse myself from deciding B039 (circuit QED), as stated in round 1; it is not in my configuration. I report no specific conflict on B045, B022 or B030 from my provided profile. I note Kroll's and Olsson's disclosures and treat them as disclosed bias, and I have no objection to the chair handling recusal on B022 or B039 as the committee sees fit.
